projects.name: Analytics Dashboard
projects.description:
A new analytics dashboard product that ingests customer CSV files, analyzes application logs, and presents results through interactive visualization components.

Scope covers three data domains:
1. Customer CSV ingestion and data processing (schema validation, normalization, aggregation).
2. Application log analysis (parsing, error/anomaly extraction, metrics rollups).
3. Visualization components and the dashboard shell that ties them together.

Work is organized as milestones with each milestone decomposed into tasks sized to be executable in roughly 1-2 days or less (complexity <= 5/10).

Tags: analytics, dashboard, data-processing, visualization

tasks.name: M1: Customer CSV Data Processing
tasks.details:
Milestone 1. Turn raw customer CSV files into clean, validated, query-ready datasets.

Outcomes:
- Repeatable CSV ingestion path (upload or folder drop) with schema detection and validation.
- Normalization of customer records (emails, dates, currency, deduplication) into canonical tables.
- Pre-computed aggregates (per-customer, per-region, per-period) that the dashboard can read directly.

Exit criteria: A sample customer CSV set flows end-to-end into aggregated tables with validation failures reported, covered by tests.

tasks.name: M2: Application Log Analysis Pipeline
tasks.details:
Milestone 2. Build the log analysis capability that feeds dashboard metrics.

Outcomes:
- Log ingestion from application log files/streams with a defined parsing format (structured JSON plus fallback regex for plaintext).
- Extraction of error events, warning trends, latency/response-time records, and request volume.
- Anomaly/error-rate detection with configurable thresholds.
- Aggregated log metrics persisted on a schedule for dashboard consumption.

Exit criteria: Sample application logs are parsed, error/latency/anomaly metrics are produced and stored, and parsing rules are covered by tests.

tasks.name: M3: Visualization Component Library
tasks.details:
Milestone 3. Deliver the reusable chart and widget components the dashboard is assembled from.

Outcomes:
- A component library of chart primitives (time series, bar, KPI tile, table, heatmap) with consistent theming.
- Each component takes a typed data contract and handles loading/empty/error states.
- Accessibility and responsiveness built in rather than retrofitted.

Exit criteria: Components are demoed in isolation with fixture data, are keyboard accessible, and are covered by snapshot/unit tests.

tasks.name: M4: Dashboard Shell, API and Integration
tasks.details:
Milestone 4. Assemble the actual dashboard application on top of the data pipelines and component library.

Outcomes:
- Backend query API serving customer and log aggregates with filtering (date range, region, customer segment).
- Dashboard shell with routing, layout, global filters, and persisted user preferences.
- Screen pages that combine visualization components with real pipeline data.

Exit criteria: A user can open the dashboard, change global filters, and see customer and log panels update from real data within acceptable latency.

tasks.name: M5: Quality, Performance and Release Readiness
tasks.details:
Milestone 5. Make the dashboard trustworthy and shippable.

Outcomes:
- Automated test coverage across pipelines, API, and components.
- Performance validation on realistic data volumes with documented thresholds.
- Deployment pipeline, observability, runbook, and a docs set for operators and end users.

Exit criteria: A release candidate is deployable through CI with green tests, documented performance limits, and an operational runbook.

tasks.name: M1.1 Define canonical customer data schema and CSV contract
tasks.details:
Goal: One agreed definition of what a valid customer CSV is, so ingestion, validation and aggregation don't diverge.

Steps:
1. Inventory the real-world customer CSV variants we receive (column names, delimiters, encodings, header quirks).
2. Write the canonical record schema: customer_id, name, email, region, segment, signup_date, currency, revenue amounts, optional custom attributes.
3. Specify per-column rules: required/optional, type, format, allowed ranges, null handling.
4. Document the CSV contract (delimiter, encoding, quoting, max file size, expected header aliases) in a short markdown spec.
5. Review the spec with whoever owns the customer data and capture agreed changes.

Definition of done: A versioned schema spec (typed model + rules table) exists in the repo, reviewed and accepted, and is referenced by M1.2/M1.3.

Complexity 4/10 - no upstream dependencies.

tasks.name: M1.2 Build CSV intake and file-level validation
tasks.details:
Goal: A repeatable way to get a customer CSV file into the pipeline and reject obviously broken files before row processing.

Steps:
1. Implement an intake entry point: upload endpoint or watched folder, per decided deployment shape.
2. Detect encoding/delimiter and map header aliases to the canonical schema from M1.1.
3. Add file-level checks: content type, size limit, empty file, missing required headers, duplicate headers.
4. Store raw files immutably (object storage or raw/ folder) with a batch ID and checksum so re-runs are traceable.
5. Emit a structured intake result: accepted/rejected + reason codes.
6. Unit tests for header alias mapping and each rejection reason.

Definition of done: A malformed file is rejected with a clear reason and a good file is stored with a batch ID; tests cover both paths.

Complexity 5/10 (single service, well-bounded). Depends on M1.1.

tasks.name: M1.3 Implement row-level validation with an error report
tasks.details:
Goal: Bad rows never silently corrupt analytics; they are quarantined and explained.

Steps:
1. Implement per-row validation against the rules in M1.1 (types, formats, ranges, required fields, email syntax, date parsing, currency codes).
2. Classify failures: reject-row vs coerce-with-warning vs drop-duplicate.
3. Quarantine failing rows into an error table keyed by batch ID + row number + reason code.
4. Produce a validation summary per batch: rows in, valid, coerced, rejected, with a sample of each error type.
5. Surface the summary through the intake result so it can be shown in the UI later.
6. Tests: one fixture per rule, plus a mixed-validity file asserting exact counts.

Definition of done: Given a mixed-quality CSV, valid rows continue downstream, invalid rows are quarantined with reason codes, and the summary counts are asserted in tests.

Complexity 5/10. Depends on M1.1.

tasks.name: M1.4 Normalize and deduplicate validated customer records
tasks.details:
Goal: One canonical customer row per customer, with consistent types so aggregation is trivial.

Steps:
1. Map validated rows into the canonical customer table (trim/case-normalize emails, ISO-8601 dates in UTC, ISO currency codes, numeric money).
2. Define and implement dedup rules: exact duplicate row vs same customer_id with a newer updated_at wins.
3. Handle multi-batch merges: decide upsert semantics and keep first_seen/last_seen batch references.
4. Expose a normalization run that is safe to re-run for a batch without duplicating rows.
5. Tests: email casing, date timezone edge cases, duplicate customer_id resolution, re-run produces identical output.

Definition of done: Re-running normalization for the same batch yields an identical canonical table, duplicates collapse to one row per customer_id, and tests assert the merge rules.

Complexity 5/10. Depends on M1.2 and M1.3.

tasks.name: M1.6 Make CSV batches idempotent and traceable
tasks.details:
Goal: Any batch can be reprocessed or rolled back without double counting in the dashboard.

Steps:
1. Add a batch registry recording batch ID, source file checksum, row counts, status (received/validated/normalized/failed) and timestamps.
2. Make each pipeline stage idempotent keyed on batch ID (delete-and-replace or upsert-by-key).
3. Implement rollback of a batch: remove its contribution from canonical and aggregate tables.
4. Prevent accidental double-ingest of the same file checksum (warn or explicit force flag).
5. Emit a lineage record so a dashboard number can be traced back to batches.
6. Tests: ingest same file twice, rollback then re-ingest, assert counts.

Definition of done: Reprocessing and rolling back a batch both leave consistent counts, verified by tests.

Complexity 4/10. Depends on M1.2 and M1.3.

tasks.name: M1.5 Build customer aggregate tables (customer, region, period)
tasks.details:
Goal: Dashboard-ready aggregates so query time never scans raw rows.

Steps:
1. Define aggregate tables: per-customer (revenue, order count, last activity), per-region (customers, revenue, growth), per-period (daily/weekly/monthly totals, new vs returning).
2. Implement incremental aggregation from the canonical table, honoring the batch semantics from M1.6.
3. Keep the metric definitions in one documented place (single source of truth) so UI labels match calculations.
4. Add a rebuild-all command for full recomputation.
5. Reconcile: assert aggregate totals equal direct sums over canonical data for a small dataset.
6. Tests: incremental run equals full rebuild.

Definition of done: Aggregates are produced incrementally and match a full rebuild on the fixture dataset, with metric definitions documented.

Complexity 5/10. Depends on M1.4.

tasks.name: M1.7 End-to-end CSV pipeline test with fixture corpus
tasks.details:
Goal: Prove the whole CSV chain (intake -> validation -> normalize -> aggregate) works and keeps working.

Steps:
1. Assemble a fixture corpus: clean file, messy-but-parseable file, one broken-per-rule file, a duplicate batch, a large-ish (10k row) file.
2. Write an end-to-end test that runs the full chain and asserts canonical row counts, quarantine counts and key aggregate values.
3. Add a golden-file comparison for the validation summary and aggregates so regressions are visible in diffs.
4. Wire the suite into the CI command used by M5.1.
5. Document how to add a new fixture.

Definition of done: One command runs the CSV end-to-end suite in CI, all fixtures pass, and failures point at the offending stage.

Complexity 4/10. Depends on M1.5 and M1.6.

tasks.name: M2.1 Define the log event schema and parsing grammar
tasks.details:
Goal: A written spec of what our application logs look like and what we extract from them.

Steps:
1. Collect representative log samples: structured JSON lines, framework default lines, stack traces, multi-line entries.
2. Specify the target event schema: timestamp, level, service, host/instance, request_id, trace_id, message, http method/status, latency_ms, error type, and raw pointer.
3. Define the primary JSON parser and the fallback regex grammar for plaintext lines, including how multi-line stack traces are folded into one event.
4. Specify severity mapping (DEBUG..FATAL) and how unknown levels are handled.
5. Document known unparseable patterns and the expected behavior for them (count as parse-failure, sample stored).
6. Review with the team that owns application logging.

Definition of done: A versioned log-schema/grammar spec exists with annotated real samples and is referenced by M2.2/M2.3.

Complexity 4/10. No upstream dependency.

tasks.name: M2.2 Implement log ingestion for files and rotated log streams
tasks.details:
Goal: Logs arrive continuously and completely, without duplicating or losing lines across rotation.

Steps:
1. Implement a batch reader for archived log files (directory scan, gzip support, line streaming with bounded memory).
2. Implement a simple live follower for appended files, tracking byte offsets per file inode.
3. Handle rotation/truncation: detect inode change or size shrink and reset offsets without re-reading everything.
4. Record ingestion checkpoints (file, offset, mtime) so restarts resume instead of reprocessing.
5. Attach source metadata to every line (file path, offset, ingest timestamp) for debugging.
6. Tests: rotation mid-stream, gzip archive, restart-after-checkpoint, ensure no duplicate events.

Definition of done: Restarting ingestion duplicates no events, rotation is detected, and offsets resume correctly in tests.

Complexity 5/10. Depends on M2.1 for the event schema.

tasks.name: M2.3 Implement log parsing and field extraction
tasks.details:
Goal: Turn raw log lines into typed events following the M2.1 schema.

Steps:
1. Implement the JSON-line parser and the fallback regex parser selected per line.
2. Fold multi-line stack traces into the event that started them.
3. Normalize timestamps to UTC (handle missing timezone and mixed formats) and map severity levels.
4. Extract HTTP method/status, latency_ms, error class and trace/request IDs when present; leave null otherwise.
5. Track parse quality: parsed count, parse-failure count, and store samples of unparseable lines.
6. Tests: table-driven parser cases from real samples, including multi-line and malformed lines.

Definition of done: A fixture log file parses to the expected event rows with a documented parse-failure rate, verified by table-driven tests.

Complexity 5/10. Depends on M2.1.

tasks.name: M2.4 Classify errors and warnings and fingerprint repeated failures
tasks.details:
Goal: Errors become countable, groupable groups rather than a wall of text.

Steps:
1. Define classification rules: level -> category (error/warning/info), HTTP 5xx/4xx mapping, exception-class extraction.
2. Build error fingerprints: normalize messages by stripping IDs, timestamps and numbers to group the same failure.
3. Store per-fingerprint counts with first_seen/last_seen and a representative sample.
4. Expose top-N errors and new-error detection (fingerprint first seen in window).
5. Tests: fingerprints stable across variable IDs; distinct errors do not collapse together.

Definition of done: Recurring failures group under one fingerprint with counts, and the fingerprinting tests cover both collapse and non-collapse cases.

Complexity 4/10. Depends on M2.3.

tasks.name: M2.5 Build latency, throughput and error-rate metric rollups
tasks.details:
Goal: The time series the dashboard charts, computed once per interval rather than per request.

Steps:
1. Define the metric set: request volume, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate (5xx share), warning rate, per service/endpoint.
2. Implement rollups over configurable buckets (1m, 5m, 1h, 1d) writing to a metrics table keyed by window + dimensions.
3. Handle sparse windows explicitly (emit zero or gap per documented choice) so charts don't lie.
4. Document metric definitions next to the CSV metric definitions so both live in one metric catalog.
5. Tests: known 100-event fixture yields exact expected counts and percentiles; sparse window behavior asserted.

Definition of done: Metrics for a fixture log set match hand-computed expected values for every bucket size, verified in tests.

Complexity 5/10. Depends on M2.2 and M2.3.

tasks.name: M2.6 Implement error-rate and latency anomaly detection
tasks.details:
Goal: Flag unusual log behavior without drowning users in false positives.

Steps:
1. Choose one simple, explainable baseline first (rolling median + configurable deviation, or fixed threshold as fallback) and document the choice.
2. Implement detection over error rate, p95 latency and request volume per service.
3. Add threshold configuration per service with sane defaults and a documented minimum-volume guard (no alerts on tiny samples).
4. Store detections with window, metric, observed vs expected value, severity and reason.
5. Add a cooldown/dedupe so one incident doesn't generate dozens of duplicate flags.
6. Tests: synthetic spike is detected, flat series is not, low-volume window is suppressed.

Definition of done: Documented, configurable detectors fire on injected anomalies and stay quiet on steady data, proven by tests.

Complexity 5/10. Depends on M2.5.

tasks.name: M2.7 Schedule recurring log metric materialization
tasks.details:
Goal: Dashboard metrics stay fresh without anyone running a script.

Steps:
1. Add a scheduler (cron-style job runner already available in the stack, or a simple loop) for the ingest -> parse -> rollup chain.
2. Make each scheduled run incremental from the last checkpoint and safe to overlap (advisory lock or single-worker guarantee).
3. Record job runs: start/end, duration, rows processed, failures, in a job-runs table.
4. Add basic backfill support: run for an explicit date range.
5. Add failure handling: retry with backoff, mark stuck runs, alert on consecutive failures.
6. Tests: lock prevents concurrent runs; backfill produces the same result as the incremental path.

Definition of done: A scheduled run keeps metrics current, is observable in the job-runs table, and backfill reproduces identical metrics.

Complexity 4/10. Depends on M2.5.

tasks.name: M2.8 Log pipeline test suite and fixture corpus
tasks.details:
Goal: Confidence that parser, metrics and detectors don't regress.

Steps:
1. Build a fixture corpus: JSON logs, plaintext logs, multi-line stack traces, unparseable garbage, a synthetic 24h series with a known injected incident.
2. Write end-to-end tests: ingest -> parse -> rollup -> detect, asserting event counts, metric values, and the detected anomaly window.
3. Add golden snapshots for top-N errors and metric series so changes are visible in review.
4. Verify parse-failure handling surfaces counts rather than silently dropping lines.
5. Add fixtures to the CI suite wired up in M5.1.

Definition of done: One command runs the log pipeline suite, covers parsing/metrics/anomaly paths, and fails loudly on regressions.

Complexity 4/10. Depends on M2.4 and M2.6 (and transitively M2.5).

tasks.name: M3.1 Choose charting library and define design tokens
tasks.details:
Goal: Agree on the rendering approach and visual language before building ten components twice.

Steps:
1. Compare 2-3 charting options against our needs (time series with brush, bar, heatmap, bundle size, accessibility, TypeScript types).
2. Decide and document the choice with the reasons, plus what we would use for the heatmap if unsupported.
3. Define design tokens: color palette (including a colorblind-safe categorical scale), spacing, typography, chart sizing, tooltip styling.
4. Decide dark/light theme strategy and where tokens are defined (CSS variables/theme object).
5. Create a one-page playground route to eyeball components during development.

Definition of done: Library choice is documented and approved, tokens exist in code, and the playground route renders sample swatches without errors.

Complexity 4/10. No upstream dependency.
